extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, philosophers of mathematics, and math educators
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for judging mathematical proofs (including very long or computer-assisted proofs), understanding and teaching mathematical intuition, and how the mathematical community accepts results. Focuses on verifiability, accuracy, social trust, pedagogy, and philosophical stances on intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability by a sufficiently patient reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional test of a proof was that a sufficiently patient reader could work through it and verify that it was correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard breaks down for proofs thousands of pages long; one may have to rely on a team of readers rather than a single patient reader. Expect practical limits on individual verification and plan for collaborative checking. Anti-pattern: assuming that a published long proof has been individually verified end-to-end by many readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance based on mutual confidence and social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof is 5000 pages long and pieced together by several mathematicians, the team's claim is based in major part on mutual confidence in each other's competence and integrity; community acceptance is based on confidence in social institutions and arrangements of the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition that acceptance can legitimately rest on trust in authors, journals, refereeing processes, and the broader community. Scoring note: evaluate both technical content and the reputational/institutional context. Anti-pattern: treating only formal verification as sufficient while ignoring community vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on multiplicity of independent approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a prevalent feeling that, with many individuals working from different perspectives, every significant configuration will be seen sufficiently often and cannot remain unnoticed for long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor results corroborated by independent lines of attack; the more varied the perspectives that encounter the same phenomenon, the stronger the confidence. Use ongoing reexamination and cross-checks to surface missed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of local errors and gaps in long proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely reasoned several-hundred-page arguments exceed human capacity to present with absolute accuracy; 'local' arguments may be not quite right—a misstatement, a gap—and can usually be patched up but are disconcerting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and plan for minor flaws in long human-written proofs. Maintain a program of continual reexamination and patching. Anti-pattern: assuming the absence of typographical or local reasoning errors without explicit checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for post-classification maintenance and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: After final classification is announced and attention moves elsewhere, some mathematicians must remain to improve and refine the text; improving exposition and repairing gaps is a major post-classification task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate resources and personnel for post-publication cleanup and consolidation of sprawling proofs into clearer, more reliable exposition. Scoring: value efforts that reorganize, shorten, or clarify long proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of computer-assisted proofs rests on trust in computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of the computer proof of the four-color theorem is based on confidence that computers do what they are supposed to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating computer proofs, consider software correctness, reproducibility of computations, documentation, and availability of code/data. Anti-pattern: uncritically accepting machine output without checksums, independent implementations, or audits.

rubrics_metrics.name: No sharp line between computer proofs and conventional proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The four-color theorem looks exceptional because of the use of computers; classification of finite simple groups looks exceptional because of length—but no sharp line can be drawn between these examples and typical proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs on dimensions like verifiability, transparency, reproducibility, and community vetting rather than on a binary computer-versus-manual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication, reputation, and citation as practical standards of establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theorem has been published in a respected journal, if the name of the author is familiar, if the theorem has been quoted and used by other mathematicians, then it is considered established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bibliographic and citation evidence, venue quality, and subsequent usage as practical heuristics for treating a result as reliable. Anti-pattern: equating 'published somewhere' with absolute correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as the opposite of rigorous
rubrics_metrics.description: One meaning of 'intuitive' is opposite of rigorous—i.e., lacking rigor, though 'rigor' itself is often defined intuitively rather than precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When labeling an argument 'intuitive' in this sense, explicitly identify the missing rigorous steps. Convert intuitive reasoning into rigorous form when formal justification is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as visual reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitive can mean visual—arguments based on visualization or physical figures (e.g., intuitive topology or geometry) that have a referent excluded from the formal version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures and visualization as aids; they can be superior for understanding but may mislead (Hahn's examples). Anti-pattern: relying solely on pictures for proof without checking formal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as plausible or heuristic conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Intuitive' can mean plausible or convincing in the absence of proof—a conjecture one might expect to be true based on general experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intuitively plausible claims as starting points for proofs or counterexamples; explicitly record the heuristics leading to the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as an acknowledgement of incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitive arguments can be incomplete: taking limits without justification or representing a function by a series without checking analyticity; the logical gap is acknowledged by calling the argument intuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the omitted theorems or conditions and either supply them or mark the statement as provisional. Anti-pattern: hiding essential hypotheses under the label 'intuitive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as reliance on physical models or leading examples (heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitive reasoning can rely on physical models or leading examples—heuristics that suggest patterns but are not proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use models and examples to generate insight but follow up with general proofs. Beware of overgeneralizing from special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as holistic/integrative understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition can mean holistic or integrative reasoning—seeing a mathematical theory 'in the large' and believing a statement must be true because of fit with other knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this integrative view to guide research, but convert the holistic sense into a chain of defensible deductive steps for rigor. Antipattern: mistaking coherence with proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical criterion: teach intuition via examples and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: We try to teach mathematical concepts not formally but intuitively—by seeing examples, doing problems, and developing an ability to think that expresses internalized ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize hands-on manipulation (coins, pebbles), problem-solving, and examples to build mental representations. Evaluate teaching by learners' ability to get 'the right answers' and display shared mental models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as shared mental representations checked socially
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental intuitions (e.g., of the natural numbers) are shared concepts—mental representations developed by experience and checked by teachers and peers; reproducibility across individuals indicates objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intuition by intersubjective agreement and reproducibility of answers; use testing and social calibration to align representations. Anti-pattern: treating idiosyncratic imagery as universally valid intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing advanced intuition through active manipulation (kinesthetic + visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-dimensional intuition was gained through interactive computer manipulation—active control combining kinesthetics and visual thinking brought the hypercube to intuitive understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking intuition for abstract objects, provide interactive, manipulable visualizations and controls; evaluate success by users' ability to manipulate and predict outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: pictures/models are helpful but can mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: While one can get much information about geometric objects by drawing pictures or building models, misuse of pictures or models can lead one astray; it takes ingenuity to invent a situation where one could go wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage use of models but accompany them with awareness of their limits; require formal checks when the risk of misinterpretation is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical stances' demands on intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Different foundational philosophies make different demands: Platonism requires an unanalyzable intuition connecting us to ideal objects; constructivism relies on intuition of natural numbers and operations; formalism attempts to eliminate intuition by focusing on formal derivations or else reduces intuition to unconscious formalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a philosophical stance, be explicit about what is taken as intuitive, how it is justified, and what it must accomplish (e.g., discovery vs. justification). Use this to interpret the role and limits of intuition in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological criterion: treat mathematics as fallible and corrigible
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than seeking indubitable foundations, give an account of mathematical knowledge as fallible, corrigible, tentative, and evolving—like other human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical claims and methods in light of their reproducibility, corrigibility, and historical development. Value mechanisms that allow correction and refinement over claims of absolute certainty.
